name: Barefoot / minimalist shoes

lead: Barefoot or minimalist shoes have thin, flexible soles, little or no heel rise and often a wide toe box. In looksmaxxing forums they come up as a habit said to rebuild foot muscles and improve stance, posture and lifting form, and so how you carry yourself.

The chain is thin flat shoes, stronger foot muscles and mechanics, then a better stance. Reviews report minimalist footwear can increase foot muscle size and strength in healthy people. No study has tested effects on posture, height or appearance.

paras: People wear them for daily walking, gym sessions and sometimes running, usually phasing in gradually from conventional shoes. Examples cited include Vibram FiveFingers and Merrell Glove. Foot strength changes build over months.

Reviews note more running injuries soon after switching and greater ankle and forefoot joint loading. Barefoot-style use also exposes feet to abrasions or punctures. Some forum users who also wear height-adding lifts raise concerns about conflicting effects on the foot.

chain: Thin flat shoes with wide toe box
angle.text: Fans of barefoot shoes say stronger feet and better mechanics carry up into better stance, posture and lifting form, and so a better look. The path runs from thin flat shoes to stronger foot muscles to a better stance. Early studies look at foot strength; links to posture or appearance have not been tested.

lead: Barefoot or minimalist shoes are footwear designed to approximate walking or running barefoot. A 2015 consensus definition describes them as causing minimal interference with the natural movement of the foot, and a 2018 paper proposed objective criteria of a sole and upper weighing 200 g or less, a heel height of 20 mm or less and a heel-to-toe drop of 7 mm or less.[1] Common features are a thin flexible sole, zero or near-zero drop, no arch support and a toe box wider than in conventional shoes; Vibram FiveFingers, Merrell Glove and Xero Prio are cited examples.[1]

In looksmaxxing communities the shoes are mostly discussed as a posture and health topic rather than a direct beauty tool. Posters on looksmax.org argue that conventional shoes squeeze the toes and weaken foot muscles, and that wearing barefoot shoes improves foot mechanics, lifting form and, by extension, how one looks.[2][3]

Published research on minimalist footwear concerns running economy, foot muscles and joint loading in healthy adults. A 2020 systematic review and later reviews summarised on Wikipedia report increased foot muscle size and strength, changes in Achilles tendon properties and mixed effects on joint loading, with early-period injuries more common.[1] No study identified examines effects on posture, height or appearance.
infobox: Thin flexible sole, wide toe box, little or no arch support
Vibram FiveFingers, Merrell Glove, Xero Prio[1]
After the 2009 book Born to Run[4]

paras: Minimalist footwear spans a spectrum. Barefoot running shoes typically have a 3 to 10 mm sole, zero drop and a wide toe box, while minimalist running shoes have a 4 to 8 mm drop and somewhat more cushioning and a toe box between barefoot and conventional styles.[1] Soles are flexible enough to roll up, and the shoes provide little or no motion control or stability support, while still protecting against hazards such as pebbles.[1]

Barefoot running attracted attention when Ethiopian runner Abebe Bikila won the 1960 Olympic marathon in Rome without shoes.[4] Interest in it grew sharply after Christopher McDougall published Born to Run in 2009, and the Barefoot Runners Society was founded in the United States that November.[4] Commercial minimalist footwear such as Vibram FiveFingers followed this wave; the brand is described in the research literature as a 'barefoot-style' shoe that some sources equate with running barefoot.[5]

Proponents of barefoot running say it reduces flat feet, plantar fasciitis and repetitive stress injuries, and that shoes have been blamed for rising injury rates; Wikipedia notes these are claims rather than settled findings.[4] Barefoot runners tend to land on the midfoot or forefoot with shorter ground contact and higher step rates, though a 2012 study of Daasanach runners in Kenya found most still favoured a heel strike.[4]

Reviews of studies in healthy people report that minimalist footwear can improve running economy, increase Achilles tendon cross-sectional area and stiffness, and increase the size and strength of foot muscles.[1] A 2023 meta-analysis found it may slightly reduce peak patellofemoral joint loads during running, while a 2020 review found greater loading of the ankle and metatarsophalangeal joint.[1] Long-term injury risk versus standard shoes is not well established.[1]

A study of young adults compared single-leg dynamic balance in Vibram FiveFingers, athletic shoes and barefoot conditions, motivated by the common equating of barefoot-style shoes with going barefoot.[5] A 2022 study examined foot and gait characteristics of toddlers in barefoot versus conventional shoes.[6] A 2019 randomised study reported higher vertical loading rates in participants after repeated barefoot running compared with shod runners, which the source notes contradicts the injury-prevention claim; evidence is limited to healthy people.[4] No trial has tested effects on posture or physical attractiveness.

Running injuries are more common in the early period after switching to minimalist footwear.[1] Barefoot running carries a higher risk of abrasions, thermal injury, puncture wounds and localised infection depending on terrain, and gradual transition is advised in the literature to avoid muscle and tendon strain.[4] Soreness near the shin and Achilles during the first days was reported by one forum poster who switched.[2]

A looksmax.org thread titled as a 'hidden health maxxing gem' claims that narrow shoes compress the toes, contribute to plantar fasciitis and bunions, and that wide-toe-box shoes restore natural foot anatomy; the poster also reports improved squat form after a week of use.[2] Replies link better foot mechanics to better posture and appearance and mention running in Vibram FiveFingers, while another user cautions that forefoot-focused running differs from the heel-strike pattern cushioned shoes are designed for.[2]

In a separate thread a user weighs barefoot shoes for health against shoes with lifts for added height, suggesting barefoot shoes for daily use and lifts for occasions such as clubbing, and asks whether alternating might harm the foot.[3]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, barefoot shoes are treated as a low-cost 'health-maxxing' habit tied to posture and lifting, and sometimes debated against height-adding lifts.[2][3]

claims.claim: Conventional shoes squeeze the toes and cause deformities like bunions and plantar fasciitis; wide toe boxes fix this.
